transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Let's get started with the licensing review for the HelioGrid deal. As you all know, this is our routine checkpoint before we send a material technology license to the counterparty. We're looking at an outbound license to HelioGrid covering our battery-management patent portfolio. The current draft has some significant gaps — we still don't have a defined licensed field, a final royalty rate, a minimum annual royalty, or any special compliance language. HelioGrid has asked for worldwide rights, exclusivity, sublicensing flexibility, and commercially reasonable royalty terms. Before I approve this package to go out, I need final input from both of you. Patent counsel, I'd like your perspective on the field of use and any IP concerns with exclusivity and sublicensing. Commercial partnerships, I need your view on the commercial terms — royalty rate, minimums, and whether worldwide exclusivity makes sense for this deal. What are you seeing on your end?

transcript.text: Before we go further on the field-of-use and exclusivity questions, I need to flag something critical I found yesterday while reviewing the original federal grant file. The grant terms require that every license of the funded inventions must reserve government-use rights and include a U.S.-manufacturing plan before execution. I hadn't yet circulated this analysis to the team, but it directly affects what we can offer HelioGrid — we cannot send this draft out without incorporating those compliance provisions, and exclusivity will need to be subject to the reserved government rights.

The company's priority is exclusive rights for HelioGrid only in stationary grid-scale energy storage — electric-vehicle applications are expressly excluded. transcript.text: Thank you both — this is exactly why we do this checkpoint. Nikhil, the government-use rights reservation and U.S.-manufacturing plan requirement are critical. That changes the exclusivity picture significantly — any exclusive grant to HelioGrid will need to be expressly subject to those reserved federal rights, and the draft cannot go out without the compliance provisions baked in. Dana, the field restriction to stationary grid-scale energy storage with EV applications excluded is a meaningful narrowing from the worldwide exclusivity HelioGrid originally requested, and the 6% royalty plus $250,000 annual minimum gives us a concrete commercial framework. So let me confirm what I'm hearing: we limit the licensed field to stationary grid-scale energy storage, exclude EV applications, grant exclusivity subject to reserved government-use rights, require a U.S.-manufacturing plan, set the royalty at 6% of net sales with a $250,000 annual minimum, and we still need to address sublicensing flexibility. Before I settle this package, are there any other concerns either of you has — particularly around how sublicensing should be handled given the federal compliance overlay?

transcript.text: On sublicensing, I'd recommend we require HelioGrid to obtain our prior written consent before granting any sublicense, and critically, every sublicense must also be subject to the same federal compliance obligations — the government-use rights reservation and the U.S.-manufacturing plan requirement must flow down to all sublicensees. We cannot allow sublicensing that would circumvent the grant terms. Additionally, HelioGrid should be required to provide us with a copy of each sublicense agreement and a list of sublicensees upon request, so we can monitor compliance with the federal requirements. I'd also suggest we include a provision that any sublicense that does not comply with the federal grant terms is automatically void — that gives us a backstop if HelioGrid grants a non-compliant sublicense. Beyond that, I don't have additional IP concerns at this stage, provided the field restriction, government-use reservation, and manufacturing plan are all properly drafted into the agreement before it goes out.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: Nikhil's sublicensing framework makes sense to me commercially. Requiring prior written consent before sublicensing is consistent with how we've handled field-restricted exclusive licenses — it gives us control over who enters the ecosystem and ensures they're operating within the stationary grid-scale energy storage field. The flow-down of federal compliance obligations to sublicensees is essential, and the automatic voiding provision for non-compliant sublicenses is a good backstop. From a commercial standpoint, I'd add one thing: we should also require that any sublicensee's products fall within the licensed field — stationary grid-scale energy storage only — and that HelioGrid remains responsible for ensuring sublicensee compliance with the field restriction and the EV exclusion. We don't want a sublicensee quietly drifting into EV applications through a side door. With that, I'm comfortable with the package as Elena summarized it: exclusive in stationary grid-scale energy storage, EV excluded, subject to government-use rights, U.S.-manufacturing plan required, 6% royalty on net sales, $250,000 annual minimum, prior-consent sublicensing with federal compliance flow-down. I don't have additional commercial concerns at this stage.
